slides.title: Owls orient toward sounds without visual guidance
body: The barn owl, **Tyto alba**, is a nocturnal predator whose auditory system converts prey-generated sound into directed head movements. **Azimuth** is horizontal direction; **elevation** is vertical direction. Head turns provide a behavioral measure of the location the owl perceives.

Kettler and colleagues recorded head orientation while presenting sounds through earphones. At an interaural delay of 100 µs, broadband noise produced turns toward the corresponding target. A 5-kHz tone could instead elicit turns toward an alternative location in the opposite hemifield.

This **phantom source** is a localization illusion, not a second physical loudspeaker. Broadband and 1.5-kHz-wide narrowband stimuli distinguished spectral effects from a change in the imposed delay. The behavior connects auditory timing ambiguity to an observable orienting decision.

slides.title: The two ears supply time and level differences
body: **Interaural time difference**, or ITD, is the difference in sound arrival time between ears, measured in microseconds. **Interaural level difference**, or ILD, is the difference in sound pressure level, measured in decibels. Neither cue is a location label at the auditory nerve.

Kettler and colleagues used ear-canal probe microphones to measure the head’s acoustic filtering. The frontal ITD map varied chiefly with azimuth; ILD varied strongly with elevation and also contained an azimuthal component. The facial ruff and asymmetric ears contribute to this filtering.

Acoustic measurements and playback tests used directions corresponding to delays of 50, 100, and 150 µs. Natural level cues reduced timing ambiguities. The familiar association of ITD with horizontal direction and ILD with vertical direction is therefore a useful specialization, not an absolute separation of behavioral functions.

slides.title: Midbrain neurons respond to restricted auditory space
body: A **receptive field** is the set of stimulus conditions that changes a neuron’s activity. Knudsen and Konishi mapped auditory receptive fields by moving a loudspeaker around the head of a lightly anesthetized owl in an anechoic chamber, which minimized reflected sound.

Noise bursts lasted 100 ms and were delivered 10 dB above each unit’s threshold. Speaker positions were sampled in azimuth and elevation while extracellular spikes were recorded. A smaller **best area** was defined by the positions producing maximal rather than merely detectable responses.

Most mapped fields were vertically elongated. Their widths ranged from 7° to 40° in azimuth, with a mean of 25°. A broad response boundary and a smaller best area describe different aspects of selectivity; neither alone is a behavioral localization threshold.

slides.title: Midbrain neighbors represent neighboring sound locations
body: Knudsen and Konishi reconstructed electrode tracks histologically and compared recording position with the center of each neuron’s best area. The auditory region was called **MLD**, nucleus mesencephalicus lateralis dorsalis, the avian homolog of the inferior colliculus.

Best-area azimuth shifted from approximately 60° contralateral in the posterolateral region to 15° ipsilateral anteromedially. Best-area elevation ranged from about +20° to −90°, with higher directions represented dorsally and lower directions ventrally. Neighboring neurons generally had overlapping receptive fields.

Tone bursts, clicks, and noise usually preserved best-area location; changing level from 10 to 30 dB above threshold also preserved its position. The orderly representation supports a computed map of auditory space rather than a simple map of acoustic frequency or overall loudness.

slides.title: Timing and level preferences can vary independently
body: A **tuning curve** relates neuronal response to a controlled stimulus parameter. Takahashi, Moiseff, and Konishi varied ITD while holding ILD fixed, then varied ILD while holding ITD fixed, recording from space-specific midbrain neurons through calibrated earphone stimulation.

Changing the level difference over a 20-dB range did not systematically displace the timing preference. Conversely, changes in timing altered response magnitude without systematically displacing the preferred level difference. The positions of the two response peaks were separable.

Independence of preferred values does not mean that both cues are irrelevant to firing rate. A neuron can respond strongly only when both are favorable. The experiments separate how each cue is represented from how the two representations jointly determine the output.

slides.title: Angularis activity is necessary for normal level tuning
body: **Nucleus angularis**, or NA, is a cochlear nucleus receiving auditory-nerve input. Takahashi and colleagues locally injected lidocaine into NA while recording a space-specific neuron in the inferior colliculus. Lidocaine is a local anesthetic that blocks neuronal impulse conduction.

After unilateral NA inactivation, the neuron’s ILD response shifted toward the injected side’s altered effective input. In the same preparation, the ITD response peak remained essentially stable. Recovery measurements and an injection-site marker linked the change to a localized, reversible manipulation.

The selective alteration supports a level-processing pathway originating in NA. It does not imply that NA alone calculates a binaural level difference: its monaural output must subsequently be compared with information from the other ear. Local inactivation also cannot identify every downstream synapse.

slides.title: Magnocellularis activity is necessary for normal time tuning
body: **Nucleus magnocellularis**, or NM, is a second cochlear nucleus receiving auditory-nerve input. Takahashi and colleagues injected lidocaine into NM and measured the same two binaural tuning dimensions used in the angularis experiments, separating neural impairment from an acoustic change.

NM inactivation altered the ITD tuning of a space-specific neuron, while its preferred ILD remained approximately unchanged. Recordings before injection, during the effect, and after recovery supplied a temporal control. Injection-site histology checked the anatomical locus of the manipulation.

The reciprocal effects of NM and NA inactivation form a **double dissociation**: disrupting one pathway selectively changes timing, whereas disrupting the other selectively changes level. This establishes functional separation at the cochlear nuclei without claiming that the final spatial response is generated by only one pathway.

slides.title: Distinct brainstem nuclei preserve different sound variables
body: The eighth cranial nerve carries auditory information from the cochlea into the brainstem. Carr and Konishi identified NA, NM, and **nucleus laminaris**, or NL, in transverse tissue sections. NL lies in the timing pathway downstream of bilateral NM input.

A neurofilament stain distinguished fiber-rich laminaris from neighboring nuclei and the cerebellar peduncle. Histology supplied landmarks for intracellular recording and tracer experiments, preventing recording depth alone from being treated as proof of a particular nucleus.

The anatomical separation is compatible with parallel timing and level computations, but staining does not measure what a neuron encodes. Functional assignments require the phase-locking, rate-level, binaural, and inactivation experiments that connect these structures to particular acoustic variables.

slides.title: Magnocellular spikes retain the phase of acoustic cycles
body: **Phase locking** means that spikes occur preferentially at a particular phase of a repeating sound waveform. Sullivan and Konishi recorded NM neurons during tonal stimulation and grouped spike times into **period histograms**, which align successive stimulus cycles.

NM neurons retained phase locking at frequencies up to 9 kHz in that study. The distributions were not identical at every frequency: spikes could occur on different cycles while remaining concentrated near a preferred position within the cycle. Timing information therefore survived without one spike per cycle.

NM rate-level functions were comparatively narrow and often changed little above spontaneous discharge. This specialization supports timing transmission to NL. A phase histogram measures temporal alignment; it does not, by itself, establish a neuron’s sensitivity to differences between the two ears.

slides.title: Angularis firing rates represent changes in sound level
body: Sullivan and Konishi measured **rate-level functions**, the relation between stimulus level and spike count, in NA neurons. Compared with NM, NA typically had lower spontaneous discharge and larger increases in firing as the level of a tone rose.

Angularis responses commonly changed over more than 20 dB, often 30 dB or more. The **dynamic range** is the range of levels over which the response changes substantially. Different cells showed different slopes and saturation levels, preserving a population representation of level.

NA showed little or no phase locking at higher frequencies, although weak locking occurred below about 3.5 kHz. The contrast with NM concerns relative specialization, not perfectly exclusive coding. Monaural level-sensitive discharge provides input for later comparison between ears.

slides.title: Auditory-nerve phase locking reaches approximately 10 kHz
body: Köppl recorded single auditory-nerve fibers with calibrated tones and compared their spike timing across frequency and sound level. **Vector strength** quantifies concentration of spike phases: values near one indicate tight phase alignment, whereas values near zero indicate dispersed phases.

Auditory-nerve phase locking extended to approximately 10 kHz. Its quality declined with frequency, but the decline included a plateau around 1.5–3 kHz. Phase organization could be detected below the level at which a clear increase in average spike rate appeared.

The peripheral temporal code supplies the brainstem with information needed for ITD processing. Detectable locking is not equivalent to equally precise locking at every frequency. Rate threshold and timing sensitivity also describe different response measurements and should not be treated as interchangeable.

slides.title: The NM synapse limits some temporal precision
body: Köppl obtained auditory-nerve and NM recordings in the same animals, permitting a direct comparison of temporal information before and after the first central relay. Tone frequency and level were controlled while saturated phase-locking quality was assessed.

Above approximately 1 kHz, NM vector strength was consistently lower than auditory-nerve vector strength. The comparison does not support a universal sharpening of phase locking at this relay. Both populations retained locking well into the frequency range used for owl localization.

The additional synaptic transformation can introduce temporal dispersion even in a highly specialized pathway. These recordings identify a functional limitation of transmission; they do not isolate a particular ion-channel subtype or determine whether convergence compensates for the loss at later stages.

slides.title: Laminaris receives frequency-matched input from both ears
body: **Tonotopy** is the orderly anatomical representation of acoustic frequency. Carr and Konishi traced NM projections and recorded afferent fibers within NL. Inputs from opposite ears entered corresponding frequency regions rather than mixing all frequencies indiscriminately.

Frequency matching permits comparison of the timing of corresponding waveform components. Comparing unrelated frequencies would not preserve a stable phase relation. Anatomical tracing establishes projection order, while the paired frequency-response measurements establish the functional matching needed by a timing comparator.

slides.title: Input spike timing changes systematically through laminaris
body: Carr and Konishi recorded phase-locked NM afferents at different depths within NL. They stimulated one ear with a tone and measured the mean phase of the resulting intracellularly recorded spikes, testing whether conduction time changed along the projection.

At 4 kHz, the tonal period was 250 µs; at 5.5 kHz it was approximately 182 µs. Mean phase changed regularly with depth. In a 7-kHz region, abrupt apparent phase jumps corresponded to crossing into the next stimulus cycle.

**Phase wrapping** occurs because phase repeats after a complete cycle even when physical delay continues increasing. The data support orderly neural delays rather than independent random timing at each site. Reading phase alone without recognizing cycle repetition would misidentify these continuous gradients.

slides.title: An ILD spectrum contributes to the vertical receptive field
body: An **ILD spectrum** is the set of level differences across acoustic frequencies at one sound direction. Euston and Takahashi measured head-related transfer functions and used them to deliver virtual sources through earphones, preserving frequency-dependent acoustic filtering.

An ILD spectrum therefore supplies substantial vertical selectivity, while timing information restricts the horizontal region. The two conditions often had different response maxima. The neuron’s normal preferred direction cannot be inferred simply by selecting the largest ILD-alone response.

slides.title: Normal spatial tuning need not maximize each ILD
body: Euston and Takahashi measured pure-tone ILD tuning across frequency and compared preferred ILDs with the values occurring at the peaks of normal and ILD-alone receptive fields. They examined bands spanning 3–5, 5–7, and 7–9 kHz.

Frequency-specific preferences matched the ILDs at the ILD-alone peak more closely than those at the normal receptive-field peak. A sum of frequency-specific inputs accounted for approximately 56% of the variance in measured ILD-alone fields, leaving substantial unexplained structure.

The normal receptive field reflects a balance of inputs rather than independent maximization of every frequency-specific channel. The reported prediction supports a contribution from spectral integration; it does not establish that the computation is purely additive or explain all inhibitory interactions.

slides.title: ICx membranes integrate timing and level before spikes
body: Peña and Konishi recorded identified ICx neurons intracellularly and labeled them with neurobiotin. A **postsynaptic potential** is a membrane-voltage change caused by synaptic input; it can depolarize toward spike threshold or hyperpolarize away from it.

Broadband noise bursts lasted 100 ms and were presented 30 dB above threshold. Testing ITD-ILD pairs produced depolarizing responses near a preferred combination and hyperpolarizing responses outside it. Spike output formed a more restricted excitatory center surrounded by reduced firing.

The intracellular measurement distinguishes input integration from the thresholded spike response. Depolarization at an unfavorable cue pair need not produce spikes. Hyperpolarizing responses support inhibition, but the recorded voltage can contain a mixture of excitatory and inhibitory influences rather than a single isolated conductance.

slides.title: Timing and level interact approximately multiplicatively
body: Peña and Konishi arranged subthreshold membrane responses into a matrix of ITD-ILD combinations. A **multiplicative interaction** means that the effectiveness of one cue depends on the strength of the other, rather than two cue-dependent responses simply being added.

After accounting for a constant membrane-voltage offset, a separable multiplicative component described about 96.6% of the response structure in the studied neurons. **Singular value decomposition** separated the measured matrix into ranked components, allowing multiplicative and additive accounts to be compared.

The analysis does not prove that one particular receptor or dendritic compartment literally performs multiplication, and it does not eliminate smaller contributions from other interactions.
